plan.english: It dawned. The father and his son went out with the dogs. The dogs tracked the boar. Under the oak the boar was lying. Then they drove it from the bed. It ran at the son. The son stood up and threw the spear. Its heart was pierced. The boar died. The father cut off its head and gave it to him, and he gave the bones to them. The son lifted it on his own shoulder. They went home. The mother saw the meat and became joyful. She boiled it.

Snow lay on the field. The king's dogs found the wolf's path in the snow. They tracked the wolf, and the king followed them. The wolf arrived at the rock. They stood around. The wolf, standing, did not flee. The king threw the spear, and it killed him. The blood was red on the snow. He flayed the wolf and placed its head on a stone. They lay down. It was getting dark.

It rained, and the dogs found the bear's path. The path led to the river. The old man, carrying the spear, followed them. The bear was swimming in the river. The old man threw it, and it went astray. Then the bear came out of the water and ran at him. The dogs seized the bear. The old man smeared the javelin with juice and struck him with it. The bear died. The old man gave the heart to them, and he laid the head on a stone. He was sweating, and he was thirsty. He was sitting down, and he drank water.

The twins climbed the mountain with the dog. It caught sight of a wolf and followed it. The wolf was swift, and it vanished. The twins were sitting down, and they were thirsty. They spoke. The wolf is swift, and the mountain is great. Let us go home. At dawn we shall come again.

Mist lay on the field. The daughter stretched the net between the stones. She was sitting down. A piglet came out of the mist and entered the net. She stood up and killed it with a stone. She cried out, and her mother heard her voice. The mother arrived, and the daughter became joyful. They pulled it home.

A bear arrived at the village and stole the sheep. The people trembled. The shepherd went to the mountain, carrying a bow. He caught sight of the bear and killed it. The people set a famous name upon him: Bear-striker. Great fame was his. His fame is imperishable.

The man threw his own spear, and it broke. The wolf set off running at him. The man became afraid. His brother seized the javelin. The javelin pierced its heart. The wolf died. Then the brother made a spear for the man.

The dogs drove the beast toward the river. It swam in the water. They did not swim. On the other side it came out. It looked at them. The stranger drew the bow and let go. It got away. Great fame was not his.

The wife cooked the meat of the boar. It was getting dark. The father sat down with the guest. He gave the head to the guest and the heart to his own wife. They ate, and they drank honey. The guest said: Father, you are a giver of good things. This meat became tasty.

The mist covered the mountain. In the mist the sister caught sight of a she-wolf. The she-wolf looked at her. The sister did not let the javelin go. She let the she-wolf go, and the she-wolf went away. The sister said to the dog: Do not run!

Two brothers arrived at the river with a net. They stretched it in the water and sat down. A beaver entered the net. The brothers stood up and seized the beaver. They killed it. They cooked it with fire, and they ate the meat and drank water.

In winter the bear was lying in the bed. The dog found the bear's bed and made a noise. The daughter heard it and arrived with her father. The bear awoke. She threw the spear, and it pierced the bear's knee. The bear fled to the mountain. The father said: He will die.

The smith took the copper and put it in the fire. He heated it. It was red. He struck it thrice. He made a spear out of it and straightened it. He gave it to the king, and the king gave him a wage. The smith's name is famous.

The carpenter found an oak and cut it. He carved a wheel out of it. He bored it with the awl. The wheel was big. He gave it to the wife. The wife yoked the cattle and drove them to the field. The wheel is strong.

The craftsman made two wheels for the lord. He joined the wheels to the chariot. The lord yoked his own two swift horses. The horses ran, and the chariot set off running. The lord became joyful. Good fame was his.
The mother was sitting. She stretched the wool, and she worked. She made a garment for her own daughter. The daughter dressed herself in the garment. In winter she did not become cold.
The husband found a stone in the field. He split it and made a quern out of it. He carried the quern home. His wife saw it and became joyful.
The carpenter built a dwelling for the lord. He set it up. The dwelling was great. The lord went into it and sat down in it.
In the field the wheel broke. The shepherd stood there and cried out. A carpenter arrived and saw it. He made a wheel. The shepherd gave him wool. Then the wheel set off running.
The man cut an oak. He carved a bow out of it. He took the sinew and stretched it on the bow. He drew the bow. He gave the bow to his brother.
The shepherd gave wool to the smith. The smith gave an awl to the carpenter. The carpenter gave a wheel to the shepherd. Whoever gives, receives.
The smith made a spear. He set a famous name upon it: Wolf-striker. The spear killed a wolf. Its name became famous. Great fame was his.
Son, hear my word! Cut the oak, and carve a bow out of it. Take the sinew and stretch it on the bow. Do not split the bow. Draw it! For whom there is a good bow, he is not afraid of the wolf.
Look at me! I grasp the oak. I cut it off. I straighten it. Now make the spear! The straight one strikes the boar. If the boar runs at you, stand and hold it up. Do not throw it at the dog.
Seek an oak. Cut it. Carve a wheel out of it. Bore through it with the awl. If the wheel breaks, do not cry out. Make the wheel again. Whichever does not break, that one is dear to the mother.

Take the wool and join it. Make a net out of it. Stretch it between stones. Sit down, and do not cry out. If the beast enters the net, stand up and hit it. Whoever sits down and does not cry out, the beast comes to him.
Son, what do you see? I see the bear's path. Follow it! Do not go to the river at night. Listen to the dog. It hears well. If it cries out, stand up. Do not flee from the bear! Hold up the spear.
Give the bones to the dog. Lead it to the water, and let it drink. Do not hit it. Whoever hits it, it does not follow that one. It is dear.
Take the copper and heat it. If it is red, strike it. If it is not red, do not strike it. Make a spear out of it and straighten it. Whoever knows the copper, his name is famous.
Daughter, sit down. Take the wool. Join it, and work. Make a garment for your sister. If you make the garment, you will not become cold in winter.
Perkwunos, hear our word! Give us swift dogs. May my spear indeed not go astray. May the beast indeed not flee from us. May we bring the meat home. Then we shall give you the heart.
Bow, become strong, bow, do not break! Bow, let the javelin go out. May the bow be dear to the king.
Net, seize the beast, hold it! May nothing flee from you, and may the net become full.
Dogs, hear well, follow the path! Do not run forward to the river. May the wolf not look at you.
Copper, become red! Copper, become an awl. Do not split. May there be fame for the man.
Wheel, run, wheel, do not break! May the two horses be swift. May the shepherd's heart become joyful.
Dawn, become bright, show us the path! May the beast indeed come to us. May we see it.
Now, wool, become a garment! May the sister become warm in winter, may she not become cold.
Perkwunos indeed slew the serpent. Wolf, go away from the field, do not come to the sheep! May the javelin strike you, may the spear strike you.
God, giver of good things, may the guest eat! May the wife eat, may we be sated.
